summary:
Project Selene is an interactive lunar exploration and decision-support platform designed to help identify and compare potential landing sites near the Moon’s South Pole. It addresses the challenges of lunar site selection by transforming complex scientific and environmental data into accessible visual insights.

The platform integrates lunar terrain analysis, elevation, surface slope, crater distribution, and Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs) to help assess landing-site safety and resource accessibility. Using interactive lunar maps and scientific visualizations, users can explore and compare candidate locations.

Project Selene leverages NASA scientific resources and datasets, including NASA Moon Trek, LROC Quick Map, JPL Horizons ephemeris data, and lunar crater databases. It also explores solar illumination conditions, the Sun’s position relative to the lunar horizon, potential solar power generation, and direct-to-Earth communication visibility windows across mission timelines.

By combining geospatial analysis, astronomical calculations, and mission-relevant environmental parameters into one platform, Project Selene aims to support more informed mission planning. It is important because the lunar South Pole presents extreme lighting conditions, challenging terrain, communication constraints, and resource-accessibility challenges. Ultimately, Selene seeks to contribute to safer, more efficient, and sustainable robotic and human lunar exploration.
details:
Project Selene – Intelligent Lunar Landing Site Analysis and Mission Planning Platform

1. Project Overview

Project Selene is an interactive lunar exploration, scientific visualization, and mission-planning platform developed to address the challenges of identifying and evaluating suitable landing locations near the Moon's South Pole. With renewed interest in lunar exploration through missions such as NASA's Artemis program, identifying safe landing sites that offer access to resources, sufficient sunlight, and reliable communication has become increasingly important.

The lunar South Pole presents several unique challenges. Its surface contains heavily cratered terrain, extreme variations in sunlight, permanently shadowed regions, and complex topography. Some areas receive sunlight for extended periods, while nearby regions remain in darkness for exceptionally long durations. These conditions directly influence spacecraft landing safety, power availability, thermal management, resource accessibility, and communication with Earth.

Project Selene aims to bring these interconnected scientific and environmental factors into one unified platform, enabling users to explore, visualize, and compare potential lunar landing locations.

2. What Does the Project Do and How Does It Work?

Project Selene combines lunar geospatial datasets, astronomical calculations, environmental analysis, and interactive visualizations to provide a comprehensive understanding of potential landing sites.

The platform is organized around several interconnected analytical capabilities:

A. Interactive Lunar Exploration and Landing Site Analysis

The platform provides an interactive lunar map that allows users to explore the Moon's surface, examine geographical features, identify candidate landing locations, and understand their surrounding terrain.

It focuses on:

  • Geographical coordinates and landing-site positioning.
  • Surface elevation and topographical variations.
  • Terrain slope and potential landing hazards.
  • Crater distribution, diameter, and depth.
  • Surface characteristics and regional accessibility.
  • Permanently shadowed regions and surrounding illuminated terrain.

These parameters help assess whether a location offers sufficiently safe and accessible terrain for a lunar landing mission.

B. Lunar Terrain and Crater Intelligence

Terrain assessment is essential for determining landing safety. Project Selene incorporates lunar topographical information and crater-related datasets to help characterize the physical environment around potential landing locations.

The platform aims to organize crater information into a structured lunar crater database containing geographical coordinates, diameter, depth, elevation, and other available terrain characteristics.

This information can help identify potentially hazardous areas, understand local surface conditions, and evaluate the surrounding environment.

Slope and elevation analysis are particularly important because steep terrain, uneven surfaces, and crater boundaries can create difficulties for spacecraft descent, landing stability, and future surface operations.

C. Solar Illumination and Sun-Horizon Analysis

One of the most important challenges at the lunar South Pole is the availability of sunlight.

Unlike many locations on Earth, the lunar polar regions experience unusual illumination conditions because of the Moon's axial orientation and local topography.

Project Selene incorporates astronomical positioning and illumination analysis to explore:

  • The Sun's position relative to a landing site's local horizon.
  • Solar elevation and azimuth.
  • Variations in sunlight over mission timelines.
  • Potential illumination periods.
  • Shadow coverage and environmental conditions.
  • Opportunities for solar energy generation.

By studying these parameters, the platform aims to estimate the potential availability of solar power at different landing locations and identify sites that may offer more favorable illumination conditions.

D. Permanently Shadowed Regions and Resource Accessibility

Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs) are areas near the lunar poles that receive little to no direct sunlight. These regions are scientifically important because they may preserve water ice and other volatile compounds.

Water ice could become an important resource for future lunar exploration, potentially supporting drinking water, oxygen production, and hydrogen-based propellant manufacturing.

Project Selene incorporates PSR visualization and lunar resource-related datasets to help users understand the relationship between potential resource-bearing regions, illuminated areas, and candidate landing sites.

The objective is to investigate how future missions might balance resource accessibility against landing safety, power availability, and operational constraints.

E. Direct-to-Earth Communication Analysis

Communication is another critical requirement for lunar missions.

A landing site may offer favorable terrain and illumination but still experience periods when direct communication with Earth is obstructed by the lunar horizon or other geometric constraints.

Project Selene uses astronomical positioning and geometric analysis to explore direct-to-Earth communication visibility windows.

Using ephemeris information, the platform aims to evaluate:

  • Earth visibility from candidate landing locations.
  • Communication opportunities across mission timelines.
  • Periods of potential communication obstruction.
  • Relationships between landing-site coordinates and Earth visibility.

This capability is intended to help identify locations and mission timelines that support more reliable communication with Earth.

F. Landing Site Comparison and Mission Overview

Rather than examining individual scientific parameters in isolation, Project Selene brings multiple dimensions of lunar site analysis together.

Users can explore different candidate locations and compare their terrain conditions, crater distribution, illumination opportunities, PSR proximity, and communication visibility.

The mission overview and analytical dashboard are designed to present important technical information through interactive graphs, scientific visualizations, maps, and organized data panels.

The goal is to make complex scientific information easier to interpret while preserving the technical details required for meaningful analysis.

3. Scientific Data Sources and Technologies

Project Selene is designed around publicly available NASA scientific resources and lunar datasets.

The principal data sources and their intended roles include:

NASA Moon Trek: Provides lunar geospatial exploration capabilities, terrain information, and access to lunar scientific datasets.

LROC QuickMap: Provides lunar surface imagery, topographical information, and visualization of lunar geographical features using Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera data.

NASA JPL Horizons: Provides astronomical ephemeris information that can support calculations of the positions and motions of celestial bodies. It is particularly relevant to modelling Sun and Earth geometry over mission timelines.

Lunar Crater Database (Robbins): Provides crater-related scientific information, including geographical locations and morphological characteristics, supporting crater distribution and terrain analysis.

Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter datasets: Provide valuable observations of lunar surface characteristics, topography, illumination, and other environmental properties.

These sources provide the scientific foundation for the platform. Different datasets must be processed, aligned, and interpreted according to their coordinate systems, spatial resolutions, time references, and scientific limitations.

4. Technical Architecture and Development Approach

Project Selene follows a modern web-based architecture intended to combine scientific data processing with interactive visualization.

The proposed technical components include:

Frontend and User Interface

  • React for building interactive user interfaces.
  • TypeScript and JavaScript for application logic.
  • Vite for development and application build tooling.
  • Interactive lunar maps, dashboards, graphs, and data visualization components.
  • Three-dimensional lunar visualization and animated scientific representations.

Backend and Data Processing

  • Node.js and Express with TypeScript for backend services.
  • API integration for retrieving and processing external scientific datasets.
  • Dedicated services for astronomical calculations and lunar data processing.
  • Data normalization and transformation to make different scientific sources compatible.

Data Storage

  • SQLite for structured local persistence.
  • A structured lunar crater database.
  • Storage of candidate landing-site information, processed parameters, and relevant analytical results.

Scientific Integration

  • NASA JPL Horizons for ephemeris information.
  • NASA Moon Trek and LROC QuickMap for lunar geospatial resources.
  • Lunar crater datasets for surface characterization.
  • Geospatial and astronomical calculations for mission-relevant analysis.

The architecture is intended to be modular so that additional datasets, scientific models, analytical capabilities, and mission-planning features can be integrated without requiring a complete redesign.

5. What Benefits Does Project Selene Provide?

Project Selene offers several potential benefits:

  1. Centralized scientific exploration: Brings different lunar datasets and mission-relevant parameters into one interface.
  2. Improved landing-site assessment: Helps evaluate terrain conditions, crater distribution, and geographical characteristics.
  3. Better power planning: Supports the investigation of solar illumination opportunities and potential energy availability.
  4. Resource exploration: Helps visualize permanently shadowed regions and investigate potential water-ice accessibility.
  5. Communication planning: Helps examine direct-to-Earth visibility and potential communication windows.
  6. Scientific accessibility: Converts complex scientific datasets into interactive maps, graphs, and understandable visualizations.
  7. Comparative analysis: Allows users to examine multiple candidate locations using a consistent set of environmental and mission-related parameters.

6. Intended Impact

The long-term objective of Project Selene is to contribute to safer, more informed, and sustainable lunar exploration.

As humanity moves towards establishing a sustained presence on the Moon, landing-site selection will become increasingly complex. Future missions will need to consider not only whether a spacecraft can land safely but also whether the surrounding environment can support long-term scientific operations, power generation, communication, and resource utilization.

By integrating these considerations into one decision-support platform, Selene aims to help researchers, students, engineers, and mission planners better understand the lunar environment.

Its broader vision extends beyond landing-site visualization towards supporting future lunar infrastructure planning, robotic exploration, resource prospecting, and human missions.

7. What Makes Project Selene Creative and Innovative?

The primary innovation of Project Selene is its integrated approach to lunar mission analysis.

Traditional scientific resources often provide specialized datasets or individual visualization capabilities. Selene aims to connect these different dimensions into one interactive exploration and decision-support experience.

Its approach combines:

  • Geospatial terrain intelligence.
  • Lunar crater and hazard analysis.
  • Solar illumination and astronomical modelling.
  • Permanently shadowed region visualization.
  • Potential resource accessibility assessment.
  • Direct-to-Earth communication geometry.
  • Mission timeline-based analysis.
  • Interactive landing-site comparison.

Instead of requiring users to independently examine different scientific resources and manually connect their findings, Selene aims to provide a unified environment in which these factors can be explored together.

The platform also emphasizes scientific visualization and usability, making complex lunar information accessible without sacrificing the underlying technical detail.

8. Factors Considered During Development

Several scientific, engineering, and usability factors influenced the project's design:

Scientific accuracy: Data sources, coordinate systems, astronomical reference frames, units, and time standards must be handled consistently. Modelled results must be distinguished from directly observed measurements.

Landing safety: Surface slope, elevation, crater distribution, terrain roughness, and geographical accessibility are important considerations.

Power availability: Solar illumination varies significantly across lunar polar locations and must be evaluated over time rather than at a single instant.

Communication reliability: Earth visibility and communication opportunities must be evaluated using appropriate geometrical models and mission timelines.

Resource accessibility: Potential water-ice regions must be considered alongside landing safety, illumination, and operational feasibility.

Data interoperability: Different scientific datasets have different spatial resolutions, formats, coordinate reference systems, and update frequencies. Integrating them requires appropriate preprocessing and validation.

User experience: Scientific information must be presented clearly through interactive maps, dashboards, graphs, and organized technical data without overwhelming users.

Scalability: The platform should support the integration of additional datasets, new landing locations, and more advanced analytical models as the project evolves.

Conclusion

Project Selene represents an effort to make lunar exploration data more connected, understandable, and useful for mission planning. By bringing together lunar terrain intelligence, astronomical modelling, solar illumination analysis, resource-related information, and communication visibility into one platform, it aims to address some of the most important challenges associated with exploring the Moon's South Pole.

Our ultimate vision is to transform fragmented lunar scientific information into a unified, interactive decision-support environment that can contribute to the next generation of robotic and human lunar exploration.
